transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Lee. Um… I guess the biggest reason I’m here is that at work, on the floor, I’m losing my train of thought constantly, and it’s starting to feel like I can’t trust my own brain in the middle of the day.

Like, I’ll be trying to work through a patient flow issue — figuring out who needs to go where, or what needs to happen next — and then an IV pump starts beeping, or someone near me asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and it’s like whatever I was holding in my head just disappears. Not just “oh, give me a second,” but genuinely gone, and I have to retrace everything to figure out what I was doing. It happens over and over, and because the floor is basically constant interruptions, I feel like I’m always getting knocked off track.
Have you noticed this kind of difficulty holding onto your train of thought throughout your life, even back in school or earlier jobs, or is this something that's really only started recently?

No, it’s definitely not just recent. I mean, work is where it feels most scary now because there are actual patients involved, but when I think back, it’s been there for as long as I can remember.

Even in elementary school, teachers would write things like, “She’s bright, but careless,” or that I wasn’t turning things in. And I remember constantly losing worksheets — like I’d do them, sometimes, or at least start them, and then they’d just vanish into my desk or backpack. Homework was a whole thing too. My mom basically had to sit with me every night and keep redirecting me, like, “Okay, what’s next? Did you put it in your folder? Did you put the folder in your backpack?” Otherwise I’d either drift off or forget to turn it in even if I’d done it.

So… yeah, the setting is different now, but that pattern of losing the thread or needing someone to keep me on track has kind of always been there.
Aside from these attention and focus issues, have you been experiencing persistent low mood, loss of interest in things you used to enjoy, or excessive worry over the past couple of weeks?

Um… I don’t think so? At least not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think. I mean, I get frustrated and overwhelmed because I feel like I’m constantly messing something up or having to work twice as hard to keep up, but I wouldn’t say I’ve been persistently sad for weeks or that I’ve stopped caring about things I normally like.

And worry… I mean, I do worry about work and whether I’m missing something, but I’m not sure if that’s “excessive worry” or just reacting to what’s happening, if that makes sense. It doesn’t feel like the main thing is mood or anxiety. It feels more like I’m exhausted from trying to keep my head organized all the time.
Do you often feel physically restless, fidgety, or have trouble sitting still, or find yourself acting or speaking impulsively without thinking it through?

Um… I don’t really know that I’d describe myself that way, no. Like, I’m not usually the person who can’t stay in a chair or is pacing around because I physically can’t stop moving. I mean, I’ll shift around or play with a pen sometimes, but I always thought that was just normal, especially during long meetings or charting or whatever.

And impulsive speaking… I’m trying to think. I don’t think people usually experience me as blurting things out or interrupting a ton. If anything, I’m more likely to be kind of stuck in my head trying to organize what I’m going to say before I say it. Sometimes I’ll talk too much once I get going — like I’m probably doing right now — but it doesn’t feel like I’m saying reckless things without thinking, exactly.

So… no, I don’t think the restless or impulsive part is the main thing for me. Or at least it’s not something I’ve noticed the way I notice the focus stuff.
Outside of work, do you notice these same kinds of attention or focus problems causing issues in other areas of your life right now, like at home, in relationships, or when driving?

Yes, definitely. It’s not just work. Work is just where the consequences feel bigger, so it’s more obvious and more embarrassing.

At home it’s things that should be so routine that I feel ridiculous even saying them. Like I’ll fully intend to call my sister or my mom back, and I’ll think, “I’ll do it after I finish this one thing,” and then it’s just gone. Or I’ll see a bill and think, “Okay, I need to pay that tonight,” and sometimes I even set a reminder, and then the reminder pops up and I either dismiss it because I’m in the middle of something or I think I’ll come back to it, and then I don’t. And then suddenly it’s late, and I’m like… how did I let that happen when I literally knew about it?

Same kind of thing with appointments. I don’t usually mean to miss things, obviously, but I’ll get the text reminder or put it in my calendar, and somehow I’ll still misjudge it or not transition to actually going. It feels like the step between remembering and doing is where everything falls apart.

And even outside of home stuff, like errands or follow-ups — if there’s a missing order or something I’m supposed to check on, I’ll have the intention, and then unless it’s right in front of my face at the exact moment, it can just disappear from my brain. It’s really frustrating because it’s not that I don’t care. I do care. I just don’t seem to reliably hold onto the task long enough to complete it.
How has your sleep been lately—are you getting enough restful sleep most nights, or do you struggle with insomnia or feel excessively tired during the day?

Um… I’m not totally sure how to answer that, honestly. I don’t think I’ve been tracking it closely enough to say in a clean way, like “yes, restful” or “no, insomnia.” Some nights I feel like I sleep okay, and other nights I don’t feel especially refreshed, but I don’t know if that’s because of sleep itself or just everything feeling like it takes more effort during the day.

I wouldn’t say I’m lying awake for hours every night in a way that feels like classic insomnia, at least not that I’ve noticed as the main issue. And I don’t think I’m falling asleep uncontrollably during the day or anything like that. I do feel tired sometimes, but I guess I haven’t really separated out whether that’s lack of sleep or just mental fatigue.

So… I don’t have a great answer. I haven’t noticed a major sleep problem, but I also probably haven’t been paying close enough attention to be completely confident.

Do you find yourself avoiding, procrastinating on, or feeling unusually reluctant to start tasks that require sustained mental effort—like detailed paperwork, charting, or planning—because they feel especially draining or hard to stick with?

Yes. That’s actually one of the biggest things I notice.

If I know something is going to require sustained focus — especially something like detailed chart review, auditing documentation across shifts, or sitting down to compare what happened on one shift to what was documented on another — I will put it off in this way that feels almost physical. Like I know it needs to be done, and I’m not confused about how to do it, but sitting down to start it feels like trying to climb a wall.

And then I’ll suddenly find all these other things that feel more urgent or more doable, especially bedside tasks. I’ll be like, “Well, I should check on this patient,” or “Let me restock this,” or “I’ll answer this call light first,” and those are real tasks, so it’s not like I’m doing nothing. But if I’m being honest, I’m also using them to avoid the thing that needs that kind of long, focused mental effort.

It’s not even that the paperwork or review is always hard intellectually. It’s more that staying with it feels so draining, and I can’t seem to get myself to settle into it unless there’s a lot of pressure or someone is basically waiting on it. Then I feel guilty, because I know I’ve been pushing it off, but in the moment it just feels overwhelmingly hard to start.
Do you regularly use caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, or any recreational drugs, and if so, has your attention or focus changed noticeably when you use more or less of them?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that in a useful way. I don’t think I’ve paid close enough attention to notice a clear pattern, like, “when I have more caffeine my focus is better,” or “when I have less it’s worse.” I mean, I probably use caffeine the way a lot of nurses do, but I haven’t tracked it in any deliberate way, and I’d be guessing if I tried to connect it directly to my attention.

As far as the other things you mentioned, I don’t have anything specific I can point to where I’ve noticed my focus changing because of using more or less of something. It’s more that my attention problems feel pretty consistently there, and I haven’t really identified a substance-related pattern. If you want, I can try to think through it more specifically, but nothing obvious comes to mind.

When you're doing something you actually enjoy or find interesting—like a hobby, a good book, or a show—do you still have trouble maintaining focus, or can you concentrate just fine in those situations?

Yeah… I think I can focus better when something is interesting, but it’s not like my attention is totally reliable even then. The bigger issue, and honestly the main reason I’m here, is what happens on the floor.

I’ll be in the middle of thinking through a patient flow issue — like who needs to be moved, what needs to happen next, what I was about to communicate — and then an IV pump starts beeping, or someone asks another nurse a question near me, or a call light goes off, and it’s like my whole thought just disappears. Not “I’m a little distracted,” but literally I’ll stop and think, wait, what was I just doing?

And then I have to mentally retrace everything: where I was standing, which patient I was thinking about, what I had already done, what I was about to do next. It’s embarrassing because the interruptions are normal hospital noises — they’re not unusual — but they derail me so fast. Even if I was focused a second before, one external thing can pull me off track, and then I’m scrambling to get back to the original thread.
Have these attention lapses ever led to an actual mistake, near-miss, or safety concern with a patient, or gotten you into trouble at work?

Yes. I mean… I hate saying that, but yes, it’s gotten to the point where work is formally involved.

I’m on supervision right now, and part of that is because people are worried about my follow-through when I’m in a charge role. It’s not like I don’t care, or I’m blowing things off on purpose — I care a lot, probably too much — but there have been enough issues with me missing steps or not closing the loop on things that other nurses now have to double-check parts of what I’m supposed to be managing.

And that feels awful. Because as charge nurse, I’m supposed to be the person keeping the big picture together and making sure nothing falls through the cracks. Instead, I feel like people are watching behind me to make sure I didn’t miss something. I understand why they’re doing it, honestly, but it’s humiliating and scary.

I don’t want to make it sound like I’m saying there was one huge catastrophic event, but the safety concern is real enough that my workplace is treating it seriously. And emotionally, it’s been really hard because I used to think of myself as reliable and capable, and now I feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader.

Yeah… unfortunately, yes. At work it’s gotten serious enough that I’m not just privately worrying about it anymore — it’s become an actual formal thing. I’m on supervision right now, and part of what they’re watching is my follow-through when I’m in the charge nurse role.

It’s hard to explain without sounding like I’m making excuses, because I’m really not. I understand why people are concerned. There have been enough times where something I was supposed to keep track of or close the loop on didn’t happen cleanly enough that now other nurses are basically having to double-check parts of what I’m responsible for. And as charge, that feels… awful. That role is supposed to mean I’m the person holding the unit together, seeing the bigger picture, making sure things don’t fall through the cracks.

Instead, I feel like people are looking over my shoulder because they don’t fully trust that I’ll catch everything. And I hate that, because I care so much about doing a good job and being safe. But the reality is, the concerns have gotten serious enough that I feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader, and that’s honestly one of the scariest parts of all of this.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. It’s not just work. Work is just where the consequences feel bigger, so it’s more obvious and more embarrassing.

At home it’s things that should be so routine that I feel ridiculous even saying them. Like I’ll fully intend to call my sister or my mom back, and I’ll think, “I’ll do it after I finish this one thing,” and then it’s just gone. Or I’ll see a bill and think, “Okay, I need to pay that tonight,” and sometimes I even set a reminder, and then the reminder pops up and I either dismiss it because I’m in the middle of something or I think I’ll come back to it, and then I don’t. And then suddenly it’s late, and I’m like… how did I let that happen when I literally knew about it?

Same kind of thing with appointments. I don’t usually mean to miss things, obviously, but I’ll get the text reminder or put it in my calendar, and somehow I’ll still misjudge it or not transition to actually going. It feels like the step between remembering and doing is where everything falls apart.

And even outside of home stuff, like errands or follow-ups — if there’s a missing order or something I’m supposed to check on, I’ll have the intention, and then unless it’s right in front of my face at the exact moment, it can just disappear from my brain. I do feel tired sometimes, but I guess I haven’t really separated out whether that’s lack of sleep or just mental fatigue.

So… I don’t have a great answer. I haven’t noticed a major sleep problem, but I also probably haven’t been paying close enough attention to be completely confident.

inference.note: Sleep question ruled out significant insomnia/hypersomnia as an alternative explanation for concentration difficulties; chronic childhood-onset inattentive symptoms across multiple settings (work, home) without hyperactivity/impulsivity or mood/anxiety symptoms continue to support predominantly inattentive ADHD. No new differential diagnoses introduced.

doctor.intent: Assess for another core inattentive-type ADHD criterion (avoidance of/reluctance toward tasks requiring sustained mental effort), which helps confirm the ADHD symptom profile and rule out purely situational or mood-related explanations.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself avoiding, procrastinating on, or feeling unusually reluctant to start tasks that require sustained mental effort—like detailed paperwork, charting, or planning—because they feel especially draining or hard to stick with?

target_item.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: If I know a task is going to take a lot of focused chart review, like auditing documentation across shifts, I keep pushing it off and finding bedside tasks to do instead because sitting down with it feels like trying to climb a wall.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about avoiding, procrastinating on, or feeling reluctant to start tasks that require sustained mental effort, such as detailed paperwork, charting, or planning.

patient.answer:
Yes. That’s actually one of the biggest things I notice.

If I know something is going to require sustained focus — especially something like detailed chart review, auditing documentation across shifts, or sitting down to compare what happened on one shift to what was documented on another — I will put it off in this way that feels almost physical. Like I know it needs to be done, and I’m not confused about how to do it, but sitting down to start it feels like trying to climb a wall.

And then I’ll suddenly find all these other things that feel more urgent or more doable, especially bedside tasks. I’ll be like, “Well, I should check on this patient,” or “Let me restock this,” or “I’ll answer this call light first,” and those are real tasks, so it’s not like I’m doing nothing. But if I’m being honest, I’m also using them to avoid the thing that needs that kind of long, focused mental effort.

It’s not even that the paperwork or review is always hard intellectually. It’s more that staying with it feels so draining, and I can’t seem to get myself to settle into it unless there’s a lot of pressure or someone is basically waiting on it. Then I feel guilty, because I know I’ve been pushing it off, but in the moment it just feels overwhelmingly hard to start.

inference.note: Continued history confirms chronic, lifelong inattentive symptoms (childhood onset, task avoidance, forgetfulness, distractibility across multiple settings) without hyperactivity/impulsivity, and mood/anxiety disorders and primary sleep disorder are ruled out as explanations, supporting predominantly inattentive ADHD.

doctor.intent: Rule out substance use (e.g., caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, recreational drugs, or medication) as a potential contributor to her concentration difficulties, per diagnostic exclusion criteria for ADHD
doctor.question: Do you regularly use caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, or any recreational drugs, and if so, has your attention or focus changed noticeably when you use more or less of them?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about substance use, caffeine/nicotine/alcohol/recreational drugs, and whether attention changes with use. The provided symptom profile does not include substance use or substance-related changes in focus.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure how to answer that in a useful way. I don’t think I’ve paid close enough attention to notice a clear pattern, like, “when I have more caffeine my focus is better,” or “when I have less it’s worse.” I mean, I probably use caffeine the way a lot of nurses do, but I haven’t tracked it in any deliberate way, and I’d be guessing if I tried to connect it directly to my attention.

As far as the other things you mentioned, I don’t have anything specific I can point to where I’ve noticed my focus changing because of using more or less of something. It’s more that my attention problems feel pretty consistently there, and I haven’t really identified a substance-related pattern. If you want, I can try to think through it more specifically, but nothing obvious comes to mind.

inference.note: Substance use ruled out as contributing factor; childhood-onset inattentive symptoms, cross-situational impairment, and task-avoidance due to sustained mental effort further support predominantly inattentive ADHD presentation. Mood/anxiety disorders remain excluded based on prior turns.

doctor.intent: Assess whether attention difficulties persist even during enjoyable or interesting activities (hyperfocus pattern), to help confirm ADHD-type inattention versus mood/anxiety-related distractibility
doctor.question: When you're doing something you actually enjoy or find interesting—like a hobby, a good book, or a show—do you still have trouble maintaining focus, or can you concentrate just fine in those situations?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: The main reason I’m here is that on the floor I lose my train of thought constantly—an IV pump beeps, someone asks another nurse a question, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve forgotten what patient flow issue I was working on.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether attention problems persist even during interesting or enjoyable activities, which most directly relates to difficulty maintaining focus and being distracted.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think I can focus better when something is interesting, but it’s not like my attention is totally reliable even then. The bigger issue, and honestly the main reason I’m here, is what happens on the floor.

I’ll be in the middle of thinking through a patient flow issue — like who needs to be moved, what needs to happen next, what I was about to communicate — and then an IV pump starts beeping, or someone asks another nurse a question near me, or a call light goes off, and it’s like my whole thought just disappears. Not “I’m a little distracted,” but literally I’ll stop and think, wait, what was I just doing?

And then I have to mentally retrace everything: where I was standing, which patient I was thinking about, what I had already done, what I was about to do next. It’s embarrassing because the interruptions are normal hospital noises — they’re not unusual — but they derail me so fast. Even if I was focused a second before, one external thing can pull me off track, and then I’m scrambling to get back to the original thread.

inference.note: Childhood-onset, pervasive inattentive symptoms (distractibility, forgetfulness, task avoidance, disorganization) across multiple settings, with better focus on interesting tasks but no hyperactive/impulsive features, no mood/anxiety disorder, and no clear substance contribution—consistent with predominantly inattentive-type ADHD presentation. No new differential diagnoses introduced.

doctor.intent: Determine whether these attention lapses have led to concrete negative consequences (e.g., errors, near-misses, disciplinary action) at work, to establish clinically significant functional impairment required for an ADHD diagnosis.
doctor.question: Have these attention lapses ever led to an actual mistake, near-miss, or safety concern with a patient, or gotten you into trouble at work?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, the concerns have gotten serious enough that I’m on formal supervision and other nurses have to double-check parts of my charge-nurse follow-through, which makes me feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the attention lapses have caused real-world work consequences, safety concerns, or disciplinary trouble, which is most directly covered by the functional impairment profile.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean… I hate saying that, but yes, it’s gotten to the point where work is formally involved.

I’m on supervision right now, and part of that is because people are worried about my follow-through when I’m in a charge role. It’s not like I don’t care, or I’m blowing things off on purpose — I care a lot, probably too much — but there have been enough issues with me missing steps or not closing the loop on things that other nurses now have to double-check parts of what I’m supposed to be managing.

And that feels awful. Because as charge nurse, I’m supposed to be the person keeping the big picture together and making sure nothing falls through the cracks. Instead, I feel like people are watching behind me to make sure I didn’t miss something. I understand why they’re doing it, honestly, but it’s humiliating and scary.

I don’t want to make it sound like I’m saying there was one huge catastrophic event, but the safety concern is real enough that my workplace is treating it seriously. And emotionally, it’s been really hard because I used to think of myself as reliable and capable, and now I feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader.

inference.note: Childhood onset of inattentive symptoms confirmed, pervasive across settings (work, home), with functional impairment; mood/anxiety disorders, sleep disorder, and substance-induced causes ruled out based on history. Presentation is consistent with predominantly inattentive presentation of ADHD.

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, the concerns have gotten serious enough that I’m on formal supervision and other nurses have to double-check parts of my charge-nurse follow-through, which makes me feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader.
target_item.reason: The doctor's last question asks whether the attention lapses have caused safety concerns or trouble at work, which is directly about impairment in occupational functioning.

patient.answer:
Yeah… unfortunately, yes. At work it’s gotten serious enough that I’m not just privately worrying about it anymore — it’s become an actual formal thing. I’m on supervision right now, and part of what they’re watching is my follow-through when I’m in the charge nurse role.

It’s hard to explain without sounding like I’m making excuses, because I’m really not. I understand why people are concerned. There have been enough times where something I was supposed to keep track of or close the loop on didn’t happen cleanly enough that now other nurses are basically having to double-check parts of what I’m responsible for. And as charge, that feels… awful. That role is supposed to mean I’m the person holding the unit together, seeing the bigger picture, making sure things don’t fall through the cracks.

Instead, I feel like people are looking over my shoulder because they don’t fully trust that I’ll catch everything. And I hate that, because I care so much about doing a good job and being safe. But the reality is, the concerns have gotten serious enough that I feel like I’m becoming a liability instead of a leader, and that’s honestly one of the scariest parts of all of this.

inference.note: Childhood onset of inattentive symptoms confirmed, pervasive across multiple settings (work, home), with functional impairment (work supervision, missed tasks) not better explained by mood, anxiety, sleep disorder, or substance use, which have been ruled out through questioning. No evidence of hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, consistent with predominantly inattentive presentation. Diagnosis remains F90.0 (ADHD, predominantly inattentive type).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of inattentiveness—losing track of tasks, difficulty sustaining attention, forgetfulness in daily activities, avoidance of tasks requiring sustained mental effort, and being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli. These symptoms are pervasive across multiple settings (work, home, relationships) and cause significant functional impairment, including formal workplace supervision due to safety concerns. Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (restlessness, physical fidgeting beyond normal, impulsive speech/action) are explicitly denied. Mood symptoms (persistent sadness, anhedonia) and pathological anxiety are also denied, making primary depressive or anxiety disorder unlikely as the principal diagnosis, though frustration and worry are present secondary to attentional impairment. No substance use pattern correlates with symptom fluctuation. The chronicity since childhood, cross-situational impairment, and predominantly inattentive presentation support a diagnosis of ADHD (ICD-10 F90.0), which encompasses attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder including inattentive presentations.
